articles.title: U.S. President and Princeton Trustee Grover Cleveland: A Beacon of Service and Integrity
articles.description: As Princeton celebrated its 280th birthday this week, Cleveland Tower's ringing bells offered more than a melodic reminder of campus tradition, serving as a resonant expression of Princeton's ideals of service and integrity, much like the building's namesake. At Opening Exercises for the Class of 2030, President Eisgruber reflected on the University as a place that "cherishes the importance of service." At the same time as the Class of 2030 begins their four-year journey, however, the University has chosen to roll back the clock after 133 years, modifying the Honor Code to allow proctoring for in-person examinations, a change spurred by the "perception that cheating on in-class exams has become widespread." This anniversary celebration, we look back at U.S. President Grover Cleveland's time at Princeton, as a model of the orange and black ideals of public service and moral integrity. Cleveland first visited the Orange Bubble during his second presidential term in October 1896 to deliver the principal address of the University's Sesquicentennial Celebration, marking its 150th anniversary. In his address, Cleveland pleaded for "more earnest participation by educated men in the political affairs of the nation." Undergraduates received the president warmly, holding a sign reading "Grover, send your boys to Princeton." According to former Princeton Mayor Liz Lempert, this warm reception led Cleveland to relocate to Princeton in his retirement, stating that Cleveland "fell in love with the town." His move was made possible by Andrew Fleming West Class of 1874, the Giger Professor of Latin and, later, the first dean of the Graduate School. Having engaged Cleveland for the Sesquicentennial Celebration, this visit sparked the pair's friendship, with West helping Cleveland purchase a colonial mansion in town. Alongside his wife, Frances Cleveland, the former president moved into his new home in March 1897. In honor of his friend, Cleveland named his new home "Westland." Built in 1854 and last sold in 2025 for $5,280,000, Westland Mansion now stands as a National Historic Landmark, listed on the National Register of Historic Places. During Cleveland's twilight years, Westland became "the mecca for undergraduate processions after triumphs in athletics or debating or other times of student jubilation," according to Alexander Leitch, Class of 1924 and former secretary of the University. Leitch noted that Cleveland was known to "come out on the porch and respond with a few pleasant words," sometimes leading "a locomotive cheer." Students would similarly visit Westland on Cleveland's birthday, every March 18; at his 70th, the Senior Council passed a resolution extending "the sincere and hearty felicitations" of Princeton's undergraduates. To commemorate the occasion, Princeton's undergraduates gave Cleveland an elaborate "silver loving cup," which currently resides in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, inscribed "A slight token of the love and esteem" felt toward him by students. During the celebration, Cleveland shook each student's hands, telling them that he felt "young at seventy because I have here breathed the atmosphere of vigorous youth." As Lempert shared, Cleveland became "a very valued member of the [Princeton] community" in retirement. Cleveland's engagement with the University extended beyond simple celebrations. He also took an active part in the campus's intellectual life and institutional development. Cleveland supervised various campus meetings, such as intercollegiate debates. As part of the Stafford Little Lecture Series, he delivered public lectures annually to full audiences in Alexander Hall, with topics ranging from "The Independence of the Executive" to "The Venezuelan Boundary Controversy" and beyond. Having brought "other eminent public intellectuals to the Princeton campus," such as Albert Einstein and Thurgood Marshall, the lectureship stipulated that "Cleveland should be its incumbent as long as he lived." Institutionally, Cleveland served as a "life trustee" to the University, elected in 1901 and providing counsel on "all matters of importance connected with Princeton." According to Leitch, Cleveland thought it "a serious thing to be a trustee of Princeton," such that he "gave painstaking attention to all the details of the operation of the University that came before the board." In this role, Cleveland solicited the funds for Carnegie Lake from Andrew Carnegie, a subject first raised during one of the steel magnate's many visits to Westland, per Leitch. Moreover, Cleveland spoke for the Board of Trustees on numerous occasions, such as at Woodrow Wilson's inauguration as president of the University in 1902. Later, in 1904, Cleveland became chairman of the trustees' Graduate School committee. Believing the Graduate College to be "laying the foundation of Princeton's largest element of future greatness," Cleveland acted as a "staunch advocate" for its establishment in the words of Leitch, going so far as to oppose then-University President Woodrow Wilson's "quad" plan, which would have reorganized Princeton's social life into residential quads and eliminated its eating clubs, for fear that the plan would have delayed the realization of the Graduate College. While Cleveland retired from public life, he maintained deep social, intellectual, and institutional engagement with Princeton, in dedication to public service. Cleveland's efforts were commemorated through his position leading the charge of Commencement's annual academic procession. According to Stephanie Schwartz, the Curator of Collections and Research at the Historical Society of Princeton, such active involvement with the University contrasts with the "quieter personal life" Cleveland lived in the town of Princeton. In an interview with The Daily Princetonian, Schwartz explained that Cleveland "often hosted small formal dinners at Westland," favoring them over dining out, to the point he was "rarely seen at restaurants and concerts or lectures in town." Sporting a preference for activities like "fishing, duck hunting, [and] billiards," Cleveland attended what is now Nassau Presbyterian Church and could be seen driving around town, having "enjoyed spending time at home with his family," per Schwartz. In June 1908, Cleveland passed away at Westland at age 71. The only U.S. president born in New Jersey, Cleveland was buried in his home state at Princeton Cemetery. A simple funeral service was held at Westland and attended by family, government officials, and Princeton friends. At the end of the service, English professor Henry van Dyke Class of 1873 closed with a reading of Cleveland's favorite poem, "Character of the Happy Warrior," by William Wordsworth. Less than a year later, a gathering at Carnegie Hall in New York City commemorated what would have been Cleveland's 72nd birthday. At the ceremony, as reported by the 'Prince,' President William Taft praised Cleveland as a "man of the highest character," one who displayed "simplicity and directness of thought, sturdy honesty, [and] courage of his convictions," in addition to "a sense of public duty that has been exceeded by no statesmen within [his] knowledge." Others noted how "Clevelandism is nothing but an expression for plain, honest, sincere living," with President Theodore Roosevelt's letter of adoration read aloud at the ceremony expressing "great admiration for the life Grover Cleveland had lived in Princeton after retiring from the Presidency." Despite Wilson's disagreements over the quad plan and the location of the Graduate College with Cleveland, reflecting on Cleveland's post-presidential service, he wrote in his President's Report that "there was an unmistakable tonic in mere association with him … He did much more than give the prestige of his great name to the university: he served it with thoughtful intelligence and conscientious devotion." The former president's last words, "I have tried so hard to do right," encapsulate such reflections on his service and character, a point reinforced by Cleveland's political moniker, "Grover the Good," born of his rejection of the robber barons of his era. At the 2018 annual Presidential Wreath Laying in Princeton Cemetery, Mayor Lempert highlighted how Cleveland "took on graft, … the patronage system, and … the party bosses of his time," and stood as "an honest man in a time of opportunism." A tribute to his commitment to public service and unwavering moral integrity, Cleveland's own grandson said that he believed that "if you served in public office, you served the public, to the exclusion of everything else." Princeton memorialized Cleveland's legacy in 1913, erecting the Cleveland Tower of the Graduate College, a monument that still stands today. At the Tower's dedication on Oct. 22, former president Taft described it as "a tower of strength and beauty and most expressive of [Cleveland's] character." Home to the Princeton University Carillon, a large set of bells, the 173-foot Cleveland Tower contains a bust of the former president on the ground floor. Alongside his gravestone, this bust is decorated annually with "beads, shells, and coins, as is Hawaiian custom," on Hawaiian Restoration Day by a delegation from the Honolulu-based Pacific Justice and Reconciliation Center, a tradition that began in 2007 and intended to remember Cleveland's support for the Hawaiian government and its queen during the 1893 coup d'etat. While over a century has passed since his death, Cleveland Tower stands as a beacon of public service and moral integrity, a physical manifestation of its namesake and Grover Cleveland's lived commitment to these orange and black ideals. Vincent Sanfedele is a staff Archivist for the 'Prince.' Please send any corrections to corrections[at]dailyprincetonian.com.
